Parts of a neuron: A neuron is the nervous system's building block, supported by glial cells. A signal comes in through the dendrites, the soma decides whether to fire, the impulse travels down the axon (sped up by the myelin sheath), and vesicles in the terminal buttons release chemicals across the synapse.
Firing a neuron: A neuron at resting potential fires only if stimulation reaches threshold, and then the action potential is all-or-none: it fires fully or not at all. Afterward it can't fire during the refractory period, and leftover neurotransmitters are taken back up (reuptake).
Diseases: Two diseases disrupt neurons in different ways. Multiple sclerosis breaks down the myelin sheath; myasthenia gravis blocks the muscles' receptors for acetylcholine. Both cause weakness, so the cause is what tells them apart.
Basics: Neurotransmitters are chemical messengers that cross the synapse. Excitatory ones make the next neuron more likely to fire; inhibitory ones make it less likely.
The chemicals: Learn each neurotransmitter with its job and what goes wrong. Acetylcholine: movement and memory. Dopamine: reward and movement. Serotonin: mood (SSRIs keep it in the synapse). Norepinephrine: alertness. GABA: the main brake. Glutamate: the main accelerator. Endorphins: natural painkillers. Substance P: pain signals.
Functions & neurons: The nervous system takes in information, processes it and responds. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry messages in, motor (efferent) neurons carry commands out, and interneurons connect them inside the brain and spinal cord.
Divisions: The central nervous system is the brain and spinal cord; everything else is the peripheral nervous system. The PNS splits into somatic (voluntary movement) and autonomic (automatic) systems, and the autonomic splits into sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest). Reflexes run through the spinal cord.
Endocrine system: The endocrine system sends hormones through the blood, so it's slower than neurons but its effects last longer. The pituitary is the master gland. Know each hormone's job: adrenaline (emergency energy), ghrelin (hunger), leptin (fullness), testosterone, estrogen, oxytocin (bonding) and melatonin (sleep).
Old brain: The old brain keeps you alive and alert. The brainstem includes the medulla (breathing and heartbeat) and the pons (sleep-wake). The reticular formation controls arousal, the thalamus relays the senses (except smell), and the cerebellum coordinates balance and movement.
Limbic system: The limbic system handles emotion, memory and drives. The amygdala processes fear and emotion, the hippocampus forms memories, and the hypothalamus controls drives like hunger: the lateral hypothalamus turns hunger on and the ventromedial hypothalamus turns it off.
Cerebral cortex: The cortex has four lobes (F-POT). The frontal lobe plans and moves (prefrontal cortex, motor cortex, Broca's area for speech); Phineas Gage's injury showed its role in personality. The parietal lobe handles touch, the temporal lobe hearing and language (Wernicke's area), and the occipital lobe vision.
Hemispheres: The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres. Each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body (contralateral control), and each specializes (lateralization): the left in language, the right in things like tone and context.
Change & damage: The brain can reorganize itself after experience or damage (plasticity), most of all in childhood. New neurons grow (neurogenesis) in only a few areas.
Brain scans: Some scans show structure (CT, MRI) and others show activity (EEG, PET, fMRI). fMRI shows function through blood flow and is more precise than PET.
The eye: Light passes the cornea and pupil (sized by the iris), the lens focuses it (accommodation), and it lands on the retina. There rods (dim light, no color) and cones (color, bright light) turn light into neural signals (transduction), which pass through bipolar and ganglion cells to the optic nerve.
In the brain: The primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe processes what the eyes send. Feature detectors there respond to edges, angles and movement, and the brain handles many parts of a scene at once (parallel processing).
Color: Two theories explain color. Trichromatic theory: red, green and blue cones, which explains color blindness. Opponent-process theory: paired opposites, which explains afterimages. Both are right at different stages.
Gestalt: Gestalt means the brain organizes parts into a whole. It groups things that are close (proximity) or alike (similarity), fills in gaps (closure), and separates a figure from its background (figure-ground).
Depth: Depth perception uses binocular cues, which need both eyes (retinal disparity), and monocular cues, which work with one eye: relative size, interposition, linear perspective and relative clarity.
Hearing: Sound waves have amplitude (loudness) and frequency (pitch). Sound moves through the eardrum and ossicles to the cochlea. Damage to the eardrum or ossicles causes conduction hearing loss, often fixable; damage to the cochlea's hair cells causes sensorineural loss, which a cochlear implant can help.
Body position: Two senses track your body. The vestibular sense, in the inner ear, handles balance; kinesthesis tracks the position and movement of your body parts.
Smell & taste: Smell (olfaction) is the one sense that skips the thalamus and connects straight to emotion and memory areas. Taste (gustation) has five basic tastes. Supertasters feel tastes more intensely, and smell strongly affects taste (sensory interaction).
Touch & pain: Touch includes several skin senses. Gate control theory says a 'gate' in the spinal cord can block pain signals or let them through. Phantom limb is feeling sensation in a missing limb.
Unusual perception: Two unusual conditions: synesthesia, where one sense triggers another, and prosopagnosia, face blindness.
Sleep & consciousness: Sleep is an altered state of consciousness, not dormancy: the brain stays active, and everyone dreams every night. Sleep moves through stages in a repeating cycle.
Circadian rhythm: The circadian rhythm is the body's 24-hour biological clock. Body temperature rises through the day, dips in the afternoon and is lowest at night. Teens and young adults tend to be evening people, older adults morning people, and artificial light can shift the clock.
Effects of sleep loss: Sleep loss hurts the whole body: weaker focus and memory, a weaker immune system, more hunger (ghrelin up, leptin down) and more fat cells, heart risks, and effects on muscles and joints.
Sleep disorders: Know each disorder by its key sign: insomnia (trouble sleeping), sleep apnea (breathing stops), night terrors (terror in Stage 3, not remembered), sleepwalking, and narcolepsy (suddenly falling asleep).
How drugs work: Psychoactive drugs change how neurons communicate. Agonists mimic a neurotransmitter, antagonists block it, and reuptake inhibitors keep it in the synapse longer. The drugs fall into four categories: depressants, stimulants, hallucinogens and opioids.
Depressants: Depressants slow neural activity. Alcohol boosts GABA and reduces glutamate; it only seems like a stimulant because of how people act. Barbiturates and benzodiazepines are also depressants.
Stimulants: Stimulants speed the body up. Caffeine and nicotine are mild; cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake, and amphetamines mimic adrenaline. The strong ones bring a high followed by a crash and cravings.
Hallucinogens: Hallucinogens distort perception. LSD can cause psychosis-like states; THC causes mild hallucinations, relaxation and time distortion; ecstasy (MDMA) is both a stimulant and a hallucinogen and can damage serotonin neurons.
Opioids: Opioids such as heroin act as agonists for endorphins, relieving pain. With continued use the brain makes less of its own dopamine and endorphins, leading to dependence, tolerance and withdrawal.
Addiction: Substance use doesn't interfere with daily life; substance abuse does. Tolerance means needing more for the same effect, withdrawal is the distress after stopping, and addiction is compulsive use despite harm.
Substance use disorder: The DSM-5 lists 11 criteria for substance use disorder, grouped as losing control, life problems, and risk and the body. Severity depends on how many criteria a person meets: mild, moderate or severe.
Split-brain patients: When the corpus callosum is cut, the hemispheres can't share information. Each visual field goes to the opposite hemisphere (crossing at the optic chiasm). Something shown to the right visual field reaches the left hemisphere, which can name it; something shown to the left visual field reaches the right hemisphere, which can't speak but can point with the left hand.
Hemisphere styles: Split-brain research showed each hemisphere's style: the left focuses on details, words and logic; the right on the big picture, tone and intuition.
